To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
SMOH mutations are found in a subset of sporadic basal-cell carcinomas (BSCs) and in primitive neuroectoderm tumors (PNET).

(a) SMOH is mutated in a subset of human sporadic basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and primitive neuroecto-dermal tumor (PNET) of the central nerve system; (b) SMOH mutations were found in 4 BCC and 1 PNET; (c) PTCH mutations were found in eight BCC and one BCC.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of sporadic basal-cell carcinomas of the human skin.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the development of basal cell carcinomas and primitive neuroectodemal tumors of the central nerve system.
the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SMOH is a tumor suppressor gene, which is inactivated by mutations in BCC and PNET.
the SMOH and the PTCH genes are both important targets for somatic mutations in sporadic BCCC and PNETs, respectively.
SMOH and GL11 are the most frequently mutated genes in BCCs and that SMOH is a target for genetic alterations in PNETs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Shh signaling is important for the growth of both BCCs and medulloblastoma.
the SMOH and the PTCH gene represent two independent targets of genetic alterations in sporadical BCCs and primitive neuroecto-dermal tumors of the CNS, respectively.
SMOH and GL11 are important targets in the pathogenesis of BCCs and that SMOH is a target of genetic alteration in PNETs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SMOH and GL11 are frequently overexpressed in sporadic Bcc and PNET, respectively, whereas PTCH is frequently mutated in both tumors.
mutations in SMO, the gene that encodes Smoh, are found in sporadic Bccs of the skin and PNETs of the CNS.
mutations of the SMOH and the PTCH genes occur independently and are not necessarily associated.
